title: Encryption at Rest and in Transit

content.title: Encryption at Rest and in Transit

blocks.content: Picture two very different crime scenes. In the first, someone is sitting in a coffee shop with a laptop, quietly capturing every packet flowing over the shared wifi network. In the second, someone breaks into a storage closet and walks out with an external hard drive full of backups.

Both are real threats against the exact same data. But the fix for one does almost nothing for the other. That is the whole idea behind encryption at rest and in transit: they are two separate locks on two separate doors, and a system that only installs one of them is still wide open.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528676-942389203.png
blocks.alt: Data moving across a network needs TLS, data sitting in storage needs disk or database encryption

blocks.content: This lesson walks through both protections, why you genuinely need them together, how encryption at rest is actually implemented in real systems, and the part that quietly matters more than any of it: key management.
1. Introduction

Whenever people say a system is encrypted, that single word is hiding two very different jobs. One job protects data while it travels across a network. The other protects data while it sits still, on a disk, in a database file, inside a backup.

["Encryption in transit: protects data while it moves, mainly through TLS","Encryption at rest: protects data while it is stored, on disk, in a database, in a backup, in object storage","Both matter, and they cover completely different attackers"]
items: Encryption in transit: protects data while it moves, mainly through TLS
Encryption at rest: protects data while it is stored, on disk, in a database, in a backup, in object storage
Both matter, and they cover completely different attackers

blocks.content: Interviewers love this phrase because it sounds simple to say and is genuinely easy to say badly. Anyone can repeat "we encrypt data at rest and in transit." Far fewer people can explain what actually breaks if you only did one of the two, or how the encryption keys themselves are protected. That second part is where this lesson spends most of its time.
2. Encryption in Transit: Protecting Data on the Move
blocks.text: 2. Encryption in Transit: Protecting Data on the Move

blocks.content: When your browser talks to a server, that conversation travels across wifi routers, ISPs, load balancers, and who knows how many hops in between. Encryption in transit means that conversation is locked, so anyone watching the wire in the middle sees only noise.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528676-919209198.png
blocks.alt: A wifi sniffer sees plaintext traffic without TLS, but only ciphertext once TLS is in place

blocks.content: The primary tool for this is TLS. It wraps the actual request and response in a layer of encryption so that a compromised wifi network, a malicious router sitting along the path, or a nosy ISP only ever sees scrambled bytes, never the actual request, password, or payload.

["A coffee shop wifi network someone else controls","A router along the path that has been tampered with","An ISP or network operator watching traffic pass through","Anyone running a packet capture on a shared network segment"]
items: A coffee shop wifi network someone else controls
A router along the path that has been tampered with
An ISP or network operator watching traffic pass through
Anyone running a packet capture on a shared network segment

blocks.content: This module already has a dedicated deep dive into how the TLS handshake itself works, the certificates, the key exchange, all of it. You do not need to repeat any of that here. The one line worth keeping in your head for this topic is simpler: TLS turns intercepted network traffic into ciphertext that is useless without the session keys.

blocks.title: In transit protection ends the moment data lands
blocks.content: TLS protects the wire, nothing more. Once a request reaches the server and gets decrypted, or once a value is written to disk, TLS has done its job and stopped being relevant. Whatever happens to that data next is a completely separate problem.
3. Encryption at Rest: Protecting Stored Data
blocks.text: 3. Encryption at Rest: Protecting Stored Data

blocks.content: Now flip the scenario. The attacker never touches the network at all. They steal a physical hard drive from a data center, they gain unauthorized filesystem access on a compromised server, or they stumble onto a misconfigured storage bucket. None of that involves sniffing traffic, so TLS never even enters the picture.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528677-652712195.png
blocks.alt: A stolen hard drive reveals plaintext files, but a stolen encrypted drive stays unreadable without the key

blocks.content: Encryption at rest is the answer here. It means the actual bytes sitting on disk, in a database file, inside a backup archive, or in an object storage bucket are encrypted, so having physical or filesystem access to the storage is not enough to read anything useful.
["A disk or SSD in a server or laptop","Database files and the indexes built on top of them","Backup archives and snapshots","Object storage buckets like S3"]
items: A disk or SSD in a server or laptop
Database files and the indexes built on top of them
Backup archives and snapshots
Object storage buckets like S3

blocks.title: Physical theft is not the only threat here
blocks.content: A misconfigured cloud storage bucket, a leaked backup file uploaded somewhere it should not be, or an insider with raw filesystem access are all far more common in practice than an actual stolen hard drive, and encryption at rest defends against every one of them the same way.
4. Why You Need Both, Not Just One
blocks.text: 4. Why You Need Both, Not Just One

blocks.content: It is tempting to think one of these two covers you completely. It does not. Each one plugs a hole the other one cannot touch.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528677-495240712.png
blocks.alt: TLS protects the network path, at rest encryption protects storage, together they leave nothing exposed

blocks.content: Encryption in transit protects data on the wire, but it does absolutely nothing for a backup file that someone downloads directly from a leaky storage bucket. That backup was never on the wire when the leak happened, TLS was never involved. And encryption at rest protects storage, but it does nothing for a request that gets sniffed mid transfer before it was ever written to disk.

{"headers":["Threat","Stopped by encryption in transit","Stopped by encryption at rest"],"rows":[["Wifi sniffing on a public network","Yes","No"],["Stolen or leaked backup file","No","Yes"],["Malicious router along the network path","Yes","No"],["Unauthorized filesystem access on a server","No","Yes"],["A misconfigured, publicly readable storage bucket","No","Yes"]]}

Encryption in transit protects data while it travels. Encryption at rest protects data while it sits still. A real system has data doing both, all the time, so it needs both protections, all the time.
5. How Encryption at Rest Actually Works in Practice
blocks.text: 5. How Encryption at Rest Actually Works in Practice

blocks.content: Encryption at rest is not one single technique. It shows up at three different layers, and real systems usually combine more than one of them depending on how sensitive a piece of data is.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528678-548678438.png
blocks.alt: Full disk encryption covers the whole volume, database encryption covers whole tables, field encryption covers single columns

blocks.content: 5.1 Full Disk or Volume Level Encryption
blocks.text: 5.1 Full Disk or Volume Level Encryption

blocks.content: This happens at the operating system or storage volume layer, below the database and below your application entirely. Think BitLocker, LUKS, or a cloud provider encrypting an EBS volume by default. Everything written to that disk gets encrypted automatically, and everything read back gets decrypted automatically, transparent to every process running on top.

It is the broadest, cheapest form of protection to turn on, and most cloud providers now enable it by default on new storage. Its weakness is granularity: it protects against someone stealing the physical disk, but once the volume is mounted and running, any process with filesystem access, including a compromised application or a rogue admin account, reads plaintext just fine.
5.2 Database Level Encryption

This lives one layer up, inside the database engine itself, often called transparent data encryption. The database encrypts its data files and backups on disk, and decrypts rows transparently for any query that is otherwise authorized to see them.

This protects database backups and raw data files specifically, which matters because backups are copied around, shipped to other regions, and sometimes forgotten in a bucket somewhere. The granularity is still coarse though, generally the whole database or tablespace, not individual columns.
5.3 Application Level Field Encryption

This is the finest grained option: your application code encrypts one specific sensitive field, like a social security number or a card number, before it ever gets written to the database, and decrypts it only when a specific authorized code path needs the real value.

The database itself, and anyone with query access to it, never sees the plaintext of that field at all, even with a legitimate database login. This is deliberately the most restrictive option, and it comes with real trade offs: you generally cannot run a SQL WHERE clause or build an index directly against an encrypted field, and every read or write path that touches that field now needs to call encryption code.

{"headers":["Level","Granularity","Performance cost","Typical use"],"rows":[["Full disk or volume encryption","Entire disk, coarse","Close to zero, handled by the OS or hypervisor","Baseline protection turned on for every server and every file"],["Database level encryption","Whole database or tablespace","Small, handled inside the DB engine","Protects data files and backups automatically"],["Application level field encryption","A single column or field","Higher, extra work on every read and write","Especially sensitive fields like SSNs or card numbers"]]}

blocks.title: These layers stack, they do not replace each other
blocks.content: A well built system usually runs all three at once: disk encryption everywhere as a baseline, database encryption for the whole dataset, and field level encryption reserved for the handful of fields that are genuinely the most sensitive.
6. Key Management: The Part That Actually Matters Most
blocks.text: 6. Key Management: The Part That Actually Matters Most

blocks.content: Here is the uncomfortable truth underneath everything above: encryption is only as strong as how well you protect the keys. If an attacker who steals your encrypted disk also finds the key sitting in a config file three folders away, the encryption bought you nothing at all.
6.1 Key Management Services

This is why real systems almost never hand code raw encryption keys directly. Instead they rely on a dedicated Key Management Service, AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, or HashiCorp Vault's transit engine are the common ones, that stores keys in hardened, access controlled infrastructure and exposes only encrypt and decrypt operations through an API.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528678-892941128.png
blocks.alt: The application calls KMS to get a wrapped key back, an attacker without access is refused

blocks.content: ["Keys live inside the KMS, backed by hardware in most providers, and are never exported in plaintext","Every encrypt or decrypt call is authenticated and logged, so you get an audit trail of who used which key and when","Access to a key is controlled the same way access to any other cloud resource is, through IAM policies"]
items: Keys live inside the KMS, backed by hardware in most providers, and are never exported in plaintext
Every encrypt or decrypt call is authenticated and logged, so you get an audit trail of who used which key and when
Access to a key is controlled the same way access to any other cloud resource is, through IAM policies

blocks.title: Application code should rarely see a raw key at all
blocks.content: The healthy default is that your application calls the KMS to encrypt or decrypt, and the plaintext key material either never leaves the KMS or exists only briefly in memory for a single operation. If you find a raw master key sitting in an environment variable or a config file, that is a design smell worth fixing.
6.2 Key Rotation
Keys should not live forever. Rotating them periodically limits how much damage a single leaked key can do, and it is standard practice for any serious compliance program.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529071-94013147.png
blocks.alt: Rotating the master key only re wraps small data keys, the bulk of the stored data is never touched

blocks.content: The obvious worry is that rotating a key should mean re encrypting every single byte of data ever protected with it, which sounds painfully expensive at scale. In practice, most systems avoid that entirely through the pattern in the next section, envelope encryption, where rotating the master key only means re wrapping small data keys, not touching the actual bulk data at all.
7. Envelope Encryption: The Pattern Almost Everyone Actually Uses
blocks.text: 7. Envelope Encryption: The Pattern Almost Everyone Actually Uses

blocks.content: Calling a KMS for every single encryption operation sounds fine until you realize a busy service might need to encrypt thousands of records a second. KMS APIs have latency and rate limits, and paying that network round trip for every single field write does not scale.
The fix is a pattern called envelope encryption, and it shows up almost everywhere encryption at rest is done seriously.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529073-562753966.png
blocks.alt: A local data encryption key encrypts the actual data, a master key inside the KMS wraps that data key

blocks.content: ["Generate a fast, local data encryption key, a plain symmetric AES key","Use that key to encrypt the actual data, fast, entirely in memory, no network call needed","Encrypt, or wrap, that small data key itself using a master key that lives inside the KMS","Store the encrypted data alongside the small wrapped key, never the plaintext data key"]
items: Generate a fast, local data encryption key, a plain symmetric AES key
Use that key to encrypt the actual data, fast, entirely in memory, no network call needed
Encrypt, or wrap, that small data key itself using a master key that lives inside the KMS
Store the encrypted data alongside the small wrapped key, never the plaintext data key

blocks.content: To decrypt later, you ask the KMS to unwrap the small data key using the master key, then use the now plaintext data key locally to decrypt the actual data. The KMS only ever handles a tiny key, never the bulk data itself, and you only call it once per record instead of once per byte.

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Fast, since the bulk data uses local AES rather than a network call for every operation","Slightly more moving parts than a single direct KMS call per record"],["The KMS only ever touches a small wrapped key, never the bulk data","Losing the wrapped key means the underlying data becomes unrecoverable"],["The master key never has to leave the KMS boundary at all","Requires carefully storing the wrapped key right alongside its ciphertext"]]}

blocks.title: This is exactly how key rotation stays cheap
blocks.content: When the master key rotates, you only need to re wrap the small data keys with the new master key. The actual encrypted data, however large, never gets touched or re encrypted at all.
8. Real World Usage
You have almost certainly used systems that do all of this without ever thinking about it, because most cloud providers turn encryption at rest on by default today.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529073-438027617.png
blocks.alt: Uploading an object to S3 with server side encryption applied automatically before it is stored

blocks.content: ["S3 server side encryption, either managed by AWS or backed by a KMS key you control, encrypts every object before it touches disk","RDS and most managed database services encrypt storage volumes and automated backups at rest by default","Most cloud block storage, EBS volumes, managed disks, and similar, ships with encryption on by default for new resources","Mobile devices and modern laptops encrypt local storage at the OS level out of the box"]
items: S3 server side encryption, either managed by AWS or backed by a KMS key you control, encrypts every object before it touches disk
RDS and most managed database services encrypt storage volumes and automated backups at rest by default
Most cloud block storage, EBS volumes, managed disks, and similar, ships with encryption on by default for new resources
Mobile devices and modern laptops encrypt local storage at the OS level out of the box

blocks.content: None of this replaces application level field encryption for the handful of fields that genuinely need it. Default storage encryption is a strong baseline everyone should have, not a substitute for deliberately protecting your most sensitive columns.
9. Worked Example: Field Encryption with Envelope Encryption via KMS
blocks.text: 9. Worked Example: Field Encryption with Envelope Encryption via KMS

blocks.content: Say your application stores a user's social security number, easily one of the most sensitive fields a system can hold. You decide plain database level encryption is not enough here, this specific field deserves application level protection with envelope encryption behind it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529074-124873996.png
blocks.alt: A raw SSN gets encrypted with a data key, that data key gets wrapped by KMS, both pieces get stored together

blocks.content: The flow looks like this: generate a fresh data key from KMS for this record, use that data key locally with a fast authenticated cipher to encrypt the SSN, then store the ciphertext together with the small KMS wrapped version of the data key. Decryption reverses the same steps.

Notice what gets stored in the database row: the ciphertext, the iv, the auth tag, and the wrapped data key. Four fields, none of them useful on their own without calling KMS to unwrap the data key first. Even a full database dump, backup file, or leaked snapshot gives an attacker nothing readable without KMS access on top of it.

blocks.title: Never log the plaintext value or the unwrapped data key
blocks.content: It is easy to accidentally log the decrypted value while debugging, or to cache the unwrapped data key somewhere convenient for performance. Both defeat the entire point of doing this. Keep the plaintext key and value scoped as tightly as possible, ideally just the few lines of code that need them.
10. The Interview Angle

"We encrypt data at rest and in transit" is one of the most commonly recited lines in a system design interview, and also one of the most commonly recited without any real substance behind it. Saying the phrase is table stakes. Explaining what actually backs it is what separates candidates.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529074-535776246.png
blocks.alt: Encryption in transit plus encryption at rest gives full coverage, but key management is the real substance behind the phrase

blocks.content: ["State clearly that in transit and at rest are two different protections covering two different attackers, not one blanket feature","Bring up TLS for the transit half without repeating the entire handshake, that lives in its own topic","For the at rest half, mention the three levels, disk, database, and field, and pick the right one for the data's sensitivity","Talk about key management specifically: a KMS, key rotation, and envelope encryption, since this is the part that shows real depth"]
items: State clearly that in transit and at rest are two different protections covering two different attackers, not one blanket feature
Bring up TLS for the transit half without repeating the entire handshake, that lives in its own topic
For the at rest half, mention the three levels, disk, database, and field, and pick the right one for the data's sensitivity
Talk about key management specifically: a KMS, key rotation, and envelope encryption, since this is the part that shows real depth

blocks.title: A line worth saying out loud in an interview
blocks.text: We would encrypt traffic with TLS and encrypt storage at rest, but the part that actually matters is key management. We would use envelope encryption backed by a KMS so the master key never leaves a hardened boundary, keys rotate on a schedule, and application code never touches raw key material directly.

blocks.content: That single answer covers both protections, explains why both are needed, and lands squarely on key management as the real substance behind a phrase most candidates only ever repeat at the surface level.
